claims.claim: GPT-3's benchmark overlap analysis used variable word n-gram lengths based on the fifth-percentile example length, with a minimum of 8 and maximum of 13 for non-synthetic tasks.
claims.notes: This describes GPT-3's analysis setup; it is not a default threshold for modern tokenizers or every benchmark.

claims.claim: GPT-3 ignored 13-grams appearing in more than 10 training documents because manual inspection found many were common phrases or legal boilerplate.
claims.locator: Appendix C → Initial training set filtering
claims.notes: The frequency cutoff is paper-specific and was used to reduce false positives from common text.

claims.claim: GPT-3's authors warn that n-gram overlap can flag background passages without the benchmark question-answer pair, and they compare performance on cleaned subsets rather than equating every match with memorized answers.
claims.locator: §4 Measuring and Preventing Memorization of Benchmarks; Appendix C
claims.notes: The paper also notes that clean subsets may differ in difficulty and distribution from the full benchmark.

claims.claim: Llama 2 matches fully verbalized evaluation inputs in the model tokenizer space and marks a token contaminated when it occurs in a shared token n-gram longer than 10 tokens.
claims.notes: This is a token-level methodology, not the same as GPT-3's lowercase whitespace-delimited word n-grams.

claims.claim: Llama 2 allows a skipgram budget of four positions and uses below-20% and above-80% token contamination to define high-confidence clean and dirty subsets for its analysis.
claims.notes: These subset boundaries are study-specific and should not be adopted as universal pass/fail thresholds.

claims.claim: Lee et al. propose exact substring matching and approximate full-document matching to detect verbatim spans and high n-gram-overlap document pairs.
claims.locator: §4.1 Exact substring matching; §4.2 Approximate full-document matching
claims.notes: The paper concerns training-data deduplication and train-test overlap; applying it to benchmark decontamination requires benchmark-aware field handling.

claims.claim: A benchmark contamination review published for GEM 2026 proposes a four-tier taxonomy: exact, syntactic, semantic and task-level contamination, and compares string, likelihood, membership-inference, LLM-prompted and benchmark-audit methods.
claims.locator: Abstract; Four-Tier Contamination Taxonomy; Detection Families
claims.notes: This is a systematic review taxonomy; individual methods still have distinct access assumptions and false-positive risks.
